title: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
text:
In 628 the Prophet Muhammad set out from Medina toward Mecca with about fourteen hundred followers, dressed as pilgrims for the lesser pilgrimage rather than armed for war. Mecca's ruling tribe, the Quraysh, with whom the Muslims had fought several battles, would not let them enter. The Muslims stopped at a place called Hudaybiyyah, outside the sacred territory, and envoys went back and forth.

The early biography by Ibn Ishaq describes the talks with the Quraysh envoy Suhayl ibn Amr. The terms seemed one-sided. The Muslims would go home without making the pilgrimage that year and could return the next year for three days. There would be a truce for ten years. Anyone from Quraysh who went over to Muhammad without his guardian's permission would be sent back, but anyone who left Muhammad for Quraysh would not. Suhayl even objected to the wording of the document, and Muhammad agreed to sign simply as Muhammad son of Abdullah rather than as the Messenger of God.

Many of the companions were dismayed, Umar among them. But the truce allowed people to travel and talk freely between the two sides, and in the following two years many more people joined Islam than before. In 629 the Muslims made their pilgrimage. When allies of Quraysh attacked a tribe allied with Muhammad, the truce was broken, and in 630 Muhammad marched on Mecca with a large army. The city surrendered with very little fighting.
lesson: A deal that looks like a concession can be a win if it secures what matters most: time, peace and the freedom to grow. Judge agreements by where they lead.
people: Muhammad, Suhayl ibn Amr, Umar ibn al-Khattab
source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, in the recension of Ibn Hisham (translated by A. Guillaume as The Life of Muhammad, 1955)
